title: Scala Exercises
description: Read each example in its lesson first. Predict the result, then check your answer. The notes explain the idea and one common mistake.

exercises.question: @main marks a starting function. println prints text. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: @main marks the starting action. Its body calls println once. Keep the indented body under the function.

exercises.question: val names a value that cannot be reassigned. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: val fixes pencils at 3. The sum produces 5 without reassignment. Use var only when reassignment is needed.

exercises.question: An s string can insert a variable with a dollar sign. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The s prefix enables insertion. $name becomes Ravi. The s before the quotes enables interpolation.

exercises.code:
@main def lesson(): Unit =
  val score = 8
  val message = if score >= 5 then "Pass" else "Try again"
  println(message)
exercises.question: An if expression can return one of two values. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The condition is true, so message receives the then value Pass. An expression that must return a value needs both branches.

exercises.question: List holds items in order. head reads the first item. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: List puts cat first. head returns that first item. head fails on an empty list; headOption is safer when it may be empty.

exercises.question: map builds a new list by applying a function to each item. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The function doubles each item. mkString adds comma-space between 4 and 6. The old list stays unchanged.

exercises.question: filter keeps items for which its function returns true. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The underscore represents the current item. Only 8 and 9 pass the test. The underscore stands for the current item here.

exercises.question: def defines a function. Its input and return type are shown with colons. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The Int input 4 is doubled and returned as 8. The returned result must match the declared type.

exercises.question: Option holds Some(value) or None. getOrElse gives a fallback. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: None has no Int inside it. getOrElse supplies 0. Calling get on None throws an error.

exercises.code:
@main def lesson(): Unit =
  val light = "green"
  val message = light match
    case "red" => "Stop"
    case "green" => "Go"
    case _ => "Wait"
  println(message)
exercises.question: match checks cases from top to bottom. _ is a catch-all case. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The green case matches Light and returns Go. Keep case lines indented under match.

exercises.code:
@main def lesson(): Unit =
  case class Book(title: String, pages: Int)
  val book = Book("Moon Trip", 24)
  println(book.pages)
exercises.question: A case class is a handy data type with named fields and value-based equality. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The constructor places 24 in pages. Dot access reads that field. copy creates a new value rather than changing the old one.

exercises.question: foldLeft starts with one value and combines it with each list item. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The fold starts at 0 and adds 2, 3 and 4. Its final total is 9. The starting value affects the final result.
